translate.output: Then, does the meaning of freedom actually not apply to individuals? I say: How can one speak thus? Freedom of a group is the accumulation of individual freedoms. Humans cannot survive apart from groups; if a group fails to protect its own freedom, another group will invade it from outside, oppress it, and seize it—then what remains for individual freedom? As someone with shallow learning like myself, how could I possibly hope to elucidate this with mere brief words? ... Are there those in the world who love freedom? Then please do not poison freedom so as to poison the world.
translate.gold: In that case, can freedom after all not be applied to the individual? I answer: nonsense, what talk is this? Collective freedom is the sum of individual freedoms. People cannot survive on their own apart from the group. If the group does not protect its freedom, then other groups will come from outside to invade it, oppress it and plunder it, and then what will be left of the individual's freedom? For one of shallow learning like me to try to explain it in a few paltry words: how can I know that it will do? … Are there people in the world who love freedom? Let them take care not to poison freedom, and thereby poison the world.

translate.output: On the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of Guangxu, the Inner Cabinet received an imperial edict: For several years, officials both within and without China have studied current affairs, with most advocating reform for self-strengthening. Recently, several imperial decrees have been issued—for instance, establishing a special examination, reducing redundant troops, revising the military examination system, and founding primary and secondary schools—all of which have been carefully deliberated and thoroughly planned, and are now only just beginning to be implemented. However, public opinion has not yet fully opened; opinions remain divided. Some, invoking their loyalty and concern for the nation, argue that old regulations must be strictly followed and new methods must be entirely rejected. The crowd clamors with empty words that offer no real benefit. Consider the present situation: if we continue to rely on untrained soldiers, limited funds, scholars without practical learning, and craftsmen without competent teachers, while strength and weakness contrast sharply and poverty and wealth are vastly unequal, how can we truly wield a simple stick to strike armored troops with sharp weapons? ... The Imperial University in the capital serves as the model for all provinces; it should therefore be established first. It is ordered that the Grand Councilors of State Affairs and the Ministers in Charge of Foreign Affairs jointly deliberate swiftly and submit a proper report. ... This edict is hereby promulgated for general knowledge. So be it.
translate.gold: On the 23rd day of the 4th month of the 24th year of Guangxu, the Grand Secretariat received the following edict: For several years now, officials at court and in the provinces have studied current affairs, and most have advocated reform and self-strengthening. Recently edicts have been issued one after another: setting up a special examination, cutting surplus troops, reforming the military examinations, establishing schools of all levels. All were examined again and again and planned most thoroughly, and it has only just been proposed to put them into effect. But attitudes are not yet open, and opinions cannot agree. Some take cover behind experience and concern for the country, holding that the old institutions must be held fast and the new methods rejected. Many mouths clamour, but empty words are of no help. Let us ask: with the situation as it is today, and the state's strength as it is, if we still rely on untrained troops and limited funds, with scholars lacking practical learning and artisans lacking good teachers, the strong and the weak set side by side, the rich and the poor so far apart, can we really make clubs to beat strong armour and sharp weapons? … The Imperial University in the capital is to be an example to the provinces and above all should be set up first. Let the Grand Councillors and the princes and ministers of the Zongli Yamen deliberate on it jointly and report properly and quickly by memorial. … Let this be proclaimed to all. Respect this.

據稟：邵伯湖西岸地土久荒，該代表等不忍棄利於地，籌辦墾殖誠不可緩。惟該岸共有地積若干？應計畆繪圖先行呈部，以便飭交揚州民政長確查。仰該代表等迅卽遵照，並妥立招股章程辦法一同呈部。此批。

translate.output: The Minister of the Interior, Cheng Dequan, submits this report. It is understood that protecting the people and safeguarding the nation makes police administration a central mechanism; selecting worthy individuals and appointing capable persons makes schools a reservoir for cultivating talent. Nanjing, now the foremost model region, must first improve all police matters thoroughly to serve as an example for other provinces. However, since our department was recently established, funding is difficult; therefore, regarding donations, we should strive for strict economy. Accordingly, the former Jiangnan Higher Police Academy has been converted into the Ministry of the Interior's Police School. We have initially recruited 240 police trainees from the Training Institute, organizing them by subject for instruction as a temporary measure to address urgent needs. As for regular class students, once funds are secured, we will conduct new examinations and recruit and educate them, thereby fulfilling the Great President's intention of promoting public happiness. We have immediately appointed Sun Runyu, Director of Police Affairs in our department, to concurrently serve as Principal of the Police School, so that the school can be established quickly, benefiting both public and private interests. The reasons for opening the Police School should be formally documented and submitted for review and implementation. This concludes the memorial.
translate.gold: Cheng Dequan, Minister of the Interior, reports as follows. I humbly consider that for protecting the people and defending the state, police affairs are the key to administration; and for choosing the worthy and employing the able, schools are the place where talent is gathered. I note that Nanjing is now the capital, and all police matters must first be thoroughly reformed before it can serve as a model for the provinces. But this ministry has only just been founded and funds are difficult, so all measures should, it seems, be as economical as possible. I have therefore converted the existing Jiangnan Higher Police School into the Ministry of the Interior Police School. It will first recruit 240 police cadets for the training institute and teach them by subject, as an emergency measure. As for students of the regular course, as soon as definite funds have been raised, they will be admitted by examination and educated, so as to fulfil the President's intention of working to advance the people's happiness. I have also at once appointed Sun Runyu, head of this ministry's police bureau, as principal of the police school concurrently, in the hope of setting it up quickly, so that both public and private interests may benefit. As to the opening of the police school, it is proper to prepare this document and request you to examine it and put it into effect. This petition is necessary. According to your petition, the land on the west shore of Lake Shaobo has long lain waste, and you representatives cannot bear to leave its profit in the ground and plan to reclaim and cultivate it. This truly cannot be delayed. But you should measure in mu how much land there is on that shore, draw a map and first submit them to the ministry, so that we can pass them on with an order to the civil governor of Yangzhou to verify. You representatives are directed to comply at once, and also to draw up proper regulations and procedures for raising capital, and submit them to the ministry together. This is the ruling.

translate.output:
Article 1: The Treaty of Nanjing, concluded on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month in the preceding Renyin year, shall continue to be observed. The old Supplementary Agreement and Commercial Regulations previously established by Guangdong have now been incorporated into the new treaty; therefore, all such prior agreements are hereby declared void.

Article 50: Hereafter, all British official documents shall be written entirely in English. For the time being, Chinese translations may still be appended as supplementary texts. However, once China has dispatched students to study English and they have become proficient, the inclusion of Chinese translations shall cease. From now on, in any matter involving verbal or textual disputes, English shall serve as the authoritative standard. The present treaty, having been carefully compared in both Chinese and English versions without error, shall follow this same principle.

Article 51: Hereafter, in all official documents—whether issued from the capital or elsewhere—references to officials and citizens of Great Britain shall never be written using the term 'Yi' (a derogatory designation for foreigners).
translate.gold: Article 1: The peace treaty concluded earlier at Jiangning on the 24th day of the 7th month of the renyin year remains in force. The supplementary treaty concluded in Guangdong and the trade regulations are now revised; since they have been incorporated into the new treaty, all the old treaties are null and void. Article 50: From now on, British communications shall all be written in English. For the time being they will still be accompanied by Chinese; as soon as China has selected and sent students to learn English and they are proficient in the language, Chinese will no longer be sent with them. From now on, whenever there is a dispute about wording, the English shall in all cases be taken as the correct meaning. The treaty now concluded, of which the Chinese and English texts have been carefully checked and found without error, is also subject to this rule. Article 51: From now on, in official documents of all kinds, whether in the capital or the provinces, the character 夷 may not, of course, be written in referring to British officials and subjects.
translate.error: The translation's use of 'The Treaty of Nanjing' in Article 1 is anachronistic, as the treaty is simply referred to as '和約' (peace treaty) in the original text, but it doesn't fundamentally alter the meaning.

punctuate.output: 赫胥黎獨處一室之中，在英倫之南，背山而面野。檻外諸境歷歷如在几下。乃懸想二千年前，當羅馬大將愷徹未到時，此間有何景物？故知不變一言決非天運，而悠久成物之理轉在變動不居之中。是當前之所見，經廿年、卅年而革焉可也；更二萬年、三萬年而革亦可也。特據前事推將來，為變方長，未知所極而已。雖然，天運變矣，而有不變者行乎其中。不變惟何？是名天演。以天演為體，而其用有二：曰物競，曰天擇。此萬物莫不然而於有生之類為尤著。物競者，物爭自存也。以一物以與物，物爭或存或亡，而其效則歸於天擇。天擇者，物爭焉而獨存，則其存也必有其所以存；必其所得於天之分、自致一己之能，與其所遭值之時與地及凡周身以外之物力，有其相謀相劑者焉。夫而後獨免於亡而足以自立也。而自其效觀之，若是物特為天之所厚而擇焉以存也者，夫是之謂天擇。天擇者，擇於自然；雖擇而莫之擇，猶物競之無所爭而實天下之至爭也。斯賓塞爾曰：「天擇者存其最宜者也。」夫物既爭存矣，而天又從其爭之後而擇之。一爭一擇，而變化之事出矣。

translate.output: Huxley, alone in a room in southern England, with his back to the mountains and facing the wilds, could see clearly through the lattice outside, as if right before him. He then imagined what scenery existed here two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Cato arrived... Thus we know that the statement 'nothing changes' is certainly not true of natural processes. The principle by which things endure over long periods lies precisely in constant change. What is seen now may be altered after twenty or thirty years, and could also be altered after twenty thousand or thirty thousand years. However, if we infer the future from past events, we see that change is endless, though its ultimate limit remains unknown. Nevertheless, although natural processes change, there are unchanging principles operating within them. What is unchanging? This is called 'natural evolution.' Taking natural evolution as the substance, it has two functions: competition among things and selection by nature. All living things follow this, especially those with life. Competition means things striving to preserve themselves. When one thing competes with another, some survive while others perish, and the result leads to selection by nature. Selection by nature means that among competing things, only certain ones survive. For such survival, there must be a reason: it is because they possess what nature has allotted to them, their own inherent abilities, the specific time and place they encounter, and all external forces around them—all of which interact and balance each other. Only then can they avoid extinction and establish themselves independently. From the perspective of its effect, such things are specially favored by nature and thus selected to survive; this is what we call selection by nature. Selection by nature chooses according to natural laws: though it selects, nothing actively chooses; just as competition appears aimless yet is in fact the utmost struggle under heaven. Spencer said: 'Selection by nature preserves those best suited.' Since things already compete for survival, and nature follows up this competition with selection, one act of competition followed by one act of selection gives rise to change.
translate.gold: Huxley is sitting alone in a room in the south of England, with hills behind and fields in front; the scenes beyond the railing are as clear as if they lay below his desk. He then imagines what this place looked like two thousand years ago, before the Roman general Caesar came. …… Hence we know that "unchanging" is by no means the way of heaven's course, and that the principle by which things endure and take shape lies, on the contrary, in ceaseless change. What we see before us may well be transformed in twenty or thirty years, or again in twenty or thirty thousand. It is only that, inferring the future from past events, change has far still to run, and we do not know where it will end. And yet, though heaven's course changes, something unchanging operates within it. What is this unchanging thing? It is called evolution (天演). Evolution is the substance, and it has two functions: the struggle of things (物競) and the selection of heaven (天擇). This is so of all things, and most evident among living things. The struggle of things is things striving to preserve themselves. When one thing contends with thing after thing, it either survives or perishes, and the result comes down to the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is when things contend and one alone survives. Then there must be a reason for its survival: its endowment from heaven, the abilities it attains by itself, the time and place it meets with, and all the forces of things outside its body must have worked together and complemented one another. Only then does it alone escape perishing and become able to stand on its own. And looking at it from the result, it is as if this thing had been specially favoured by heaven and selected to survive: this is what is called the selection of heaven. The selection of heaven is selection by nature: it selects, yet no one selects; just as the struggle of things seems to be no struggle, and is in truth the fiercest struggle in the world. Spencer said: "The selection of heaven is the preservation of the fittest." Since things struggle to survive, and heaven then selects among them after their struggle, with each struggle and each selection, change comes about.
translate.error: The translation renders '愷徹' as Cato, when the original text refers to the Roman general Catus, a historical figure; this is a minor error as both are Roman generals, but alters the specificity of the reference.

中國政治與文化之變革，莫劇於殷周之際。殷周間之大變革，自其表言之，不過一姓一家之興亡與都邑之移轉；自其裏言之，則舊制度廢而新制度興，舊文化廢而新文化興。又自其表言之，則古聖人之所以取天下及所以守之者，若無以異於後世之帝王；而自其裏言之，則其制度文物與其立制之本意，乃出於萬世治安之大計，其心術與規摹，迥非後世帝王所能夢見也。欲觀周之所以定天下，必自其制度始矣。

周人制度之大異於商者：一曰立子立嫡之制，由是而生宗法及喪服之制，並由是而有封建子弟之制、君天子臣諸侯之制；二曰廟數之制；三曰同姓不婚之制。此數者皆周之所以綱紀天下，其旨則在納上下於道德，而合天子、諸侯、卿大夫、士、庶民以成一道德之團體。周公制作之本意實在於此。此非穿鑿附會之言也。茲篇所論皆有事實爲之根據，試略述之。

其條例則《春秋左氏傳》之說曰：「太子死，有母弟則立之；無則立長。年鈞擇賢，義鈞則卜。」公羊家之說曰：「禮嫡夫人無子，立右媵；右媵無子，立左媵。」此二說中，後說尤爲詳密。顧皆後儒充類之說，當立法之初，未必窮其變至此。然所謂「立子以貴不以長，立適以長不以賢」者，乃傳子法之精髓；當時雖未必有此語，固已用此意矣。

translate.output: The transformation of Chinese politics and culture was no more profound than between the Yin and Zhou dynasties. ... Regarding the great transformation between Yin and Zhou, if viewed from the surface, it is merely the rise and fall of one family and the relocation of the capital; if viewed from within, old systems were abolished and new ones established, old culture discarded and new culture emerged. Again, from the surface perspective, the ancient sages' methods for acquiring and maintaining rule seem no different from later emperors; but from the inner perspective, their institutions, cultural artifacts, and the original intent behind establishing them were designed for universal social stability, with moral principles and planning far beyond what later emperors could even imagine. To understand how Zhou stabilized the world, one must begin with its institutions. The major differences between Zhou systems and Shang are: first, the system of establishing sons as heirs through the principle of primogeniture, from which arose the clan system and mourning attire regulations, and also the feudal system for appointing royal relatives and the hierarchy where the emperor rules over vassal lords; second, the system of ancestral temple counts; third, the prohibition against marriage between same-surname relatives. These three principles formed the framework through which Zhou governed the world. Their purpose was to integrate all levels of society into moral order, uniting the emperor, vassal lords, ministers, nobles, and common people into a single moral community. The original intent behind Duke of Zhou's institutional creations lies precisely here. This is not forced or fabricated interpretation; the arguments in this essay are grounded in historical facts, which I will briefly outline. ... Regarding the regulations, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Zuo Commentary) states: 'If the crown prince dies, establish his younger full brother; if none exists, establish the eldest son. If ages are equal, choose the more capable one; if moral standing is equal, resort to divination.' The Gongyang School argues: 'According to ritual, if the primary consort bears no son, establish the right concubine; if she bears no son, establish the left concubine, ...' Between these two interpretations, the latter is more detailed, yet both represent later scholars extrapolating from incomplete records. When laws were first established, such elaborate variations may not have been fully anticipated. Nevertheless, the core principle 'establish sons based on rank rather than age, and heirs based on seniority rather than virtue' captures the essence of hereditary succession; although this exact phrasing may not have existed at the time, its underlying logic was already in practice.
translate.gold: Of all the changes in China's government and culture, none is more drastic than that at the transition from Shang to Zhou. …… The great change between Shang and Zhou, seen from the surface, was no more than the rise and fall of one family and the moving of the capital; seen from within, old institutions fell and new institutions arose, old culture fell and new culture arose. Again, seen from the surface, the ways in which the ancient sages won the empire and kept it seem no different from those of later emperors; but seen from within, their institutions, their culture and their original intention in founding the institutions came in fact from a grand plan for order and peace for ten thousand generations, and their thinking and design were far beyond anything later emperors could dream of. If one wishes to see how the Zhou settled the empire, one must begin from its institutions. The Zhou institutions that differ greatly from the Shang are, first, the institution of succession by the son and by the son of the principal wife, from which arose the lineage system and the mourning system, and from which came the enfeoffment of sons and younger brothers and the system in which the Son of Heaven is lord and the feudal lords are subjects; second, the number of ancestral temples; third, the rule that those of the same surname do not marry. These are all the means by which the Zhou gave order to the empire. Their purpose was to bring high and low within morality, and to unite the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, great officers, gentlemen and the common people into one moral community. The Duke of Zhou's original intention in making institutions truly lay here. These are not far-fetched or forced words: everything this essay argues has facts as its evidence. Let me set it out briefly. …… The rules are given in the account of the *Zuo Commentary*: "When the heir dies, if there is a younger brother by the same mother, he is made heir; if not, the eldest is made heir. If they are equal in age, the worthiest is chosen; if equal in merit, the matter is divined." The Gongyang school's account says: "By the rites, if the principal wife has no son, the son of the right secondary wife is made heir; if the right secondary wife has no son, the son of the left secondary wife is made heir; ……" Of these two accounts, the latter is especially detailed, but both are the extrapolations of later Confucians; when the rule was first laid down, its makers did not necessarily work out every case in this way. Yet what is called "a son is made heir by rank, not by age; the son of the principal wife is made heir by age, not by worth" is the essence of the rule of succession by sons; though these words may not have been said at the time, the idea was certainly already in use.
translate.error: The translation misses the nuance that the 'ancient sages' methods for acquiring and maintaining rule *seem* no different from later emperors, but are actually fundamentally different when examined more closely, which is a key distinction made in the original.

translate.output: My younger brother has long been a friend of Mr. Jifang, and through him I have heard of Yuanfang's virtue; I had hoped to meet him for my own satisfaction. Yesterday, while in Huicheng, I happened to encounter him, and found that your elder brother's talent and bearing surpass even what I had heard. I regret that our meeting came so late; unexpectedly, after one night we parted, and now I lament the speed of our separation. After parting, on the fourth day I arrived at Tianjin, and on the tenth day I went to Pingshu. In less than a lunar month, I have already changed two places. Tired by wind and dust, I am merely cultivating in the fields of an ordinary person; I pity myself and find it somewhat laughable. Now that my fellow scholars return home, I am the only one left in the residence; moreover, with the clear bell and red fish, it is as if I were practicing cultivation in an ancient temple. Yet the west wind and yellow leaves stir memories of our past journeys; surely the gift of the double carp will not abandon me. Is your health fully restored? With wedding affairs bringing much trouble, please take good care of yourself. Sending this by way of the wind to convey my thoughts; there is much more I wish to express. Long without seeing the grace of green wutong and bamboo, whenever the moon shines bright and the breeze is clear, I deeply long for you. Moreover, I have been puzzled by your prolonged absence from court duty. Recently I received a letter from Mr. Ruan Xihou, learning that you have traveled to the left of Mount Qi; planting lotus in Chuqiu has already been ongoing for more than a day. Green reeds and jade-like treasures are sold everywhere; this is naturally so. Your younger brother's talent and spirit: one surely believed that Jishan's solitary crane would suffice to lift the spirits of the chicken flock; who expected that the zither was broken and the grass on the grave had already grown overnight, causing deep sighs! My younger brother first lodged in western Liaoning, then traveled to Tianjin. This spring again there was the campaign at Pingshu. Year after year pressing along the line, still working as a hired hand; this is truly because village women with beautiful brows are hard for the times to appreciate.
translate.gold: I, your younger brother, formerly had the good fortune to make friends with your younger brother, and so heard of your worth as the elder, and longed for the pleasure of meeting you. Yesterday I met you by chance in the provincial capital, and felt that your talent and bearing surpassed even what I had heard. Just as I was regretting that we had not met sooner, we unexpectedly parted after a single night, and now I regret that we were separated so soon. After we parted, I reached Tianjin on the fourth and went to Pingshu on the tenth: in less than a month I have changed place twice. Travel-worn, I do nothing but weed other people's fields; I pity myself, and can also laugh at myself. Just now my colleagues have gone home, and I live alone in the office; add the clear chime and the red wooden fish, and it is just like an old temple for religious practice. With the west wind and the yellow leaves, I often long for you deeply; you will surely not abandon me, but will send me a letter. Have you recovered your health? With the wedding arrangements so many and tiring, please take good care of yourself. I send my thoughts by the wind, and cannot express all I feel. I have long not seen your bearing, like green parasol trees and jade bamboo; whenever the moon is bright and the wind clear, I long for you in spirit. I had wondered why you had not been on duty for so long. Recently I received a letter from Ruan Xihou and learnt that you have travelled to Shandong and have long been serving in a secretariat at Chuqiu. Fine swords and fine jade are sought after everywhere: that is only to be expected. Your younger brother's talent and spirit, I was sure, like Ji Shao, the lone crane, would shine among the flock of chickens. Who could have expected that Boya's zither would be broken, and that the grass on the grave is already a year old? It moves one to sorrow! I, your younger brother, first lived in Liaoxi, then soon moved to Tianjin and its lakes. This spring I have again taken up a post at Pingshu. Year after year I sew for others, still a hired hand: truly because a village girl's fine eyebrows are hard for the age to admire.
translate.error: The translation renders "雙鯉之頒" as "the gift of the double carp," which misses the nuance of a shared, perhaps reciprocal, gift or favor, rather than a simple present.
